a: The proverbs
p: Mashal covers far more than a short saying: a comparison, a parable, a poem, even a taunt.
b: The Hebrew mishle is the plural of mashal, probably from a root meaning 'be like': a proverb sets two things side by side so that one explains the other ("Like cold water to a thirsty throat..."). The same word names Balaam's oracles (Numbers 23:7), a taunt song (Isaiah 14:4), a parable (Ezekiel 17:2) and a byword (Deuteronomy 28:37). So the title promises more than one-liners. Chapters 1–9 are not proverbs in the narrow sense at all but long speeches and poems. The heading also gives the Hebrew name of the book, Mishle. The Greek begins Paroimiai Salomontos, from which the Latin and English titles come.

a: Solomon son of David, king of Israel
t: Why Solomon's name stands at the head
p: The book credits Solomon, but names other authors inside it: the wise, Hezekiah's men, Agur and Lemuel.
b: 1 Kings remembers Solomon as Israel's model sage: God gave him "a heart that is wise and understanding" (1 Kings 3:12), and "Three thousand proverbs came from his lips" (1 Kings 4:32). Yet Proverbs itself names other sources: "the words of the wise" (22:17; 24:23), "the men of Hezekiah" who copied Solomon's proverbs two centuries later (25:1), Agur (30:1) and Lemuel's mother (31:1). Many readers take 1:1 as the title of the whole book, much as the Psalms are called David's though many are by others. Others think 1:1 belongs to chapters 1–9 only, which most scholars date later than the Solomon collections (see the book's opening pages). Either way, the heading puts the book under the name of Israel's wise king and of the line of David.

a: discipline
p: Musar is training that shapes a person, by words and, when needed, by punishment.
b: Musar comes from yasar, 'to discipline, correct, train'. It can mean verbal teaching (1:8; 4:1), a warning, or the pain of correction (3:11–12; 13:24; 22:15). English versions switch between 'instruction', 'discipline' and 'correction', which hides that one word runs through the book about thirty times. The Plain keeps 'discipline' throughout, so readers can follow it. The idea is that wisdom is not just information. It is learned under authority, the way a son learns from a father, and it often hurts (Hebrews 12:11 says the same of God's discipline). The Greek translates it paideia, 'education, upbringing', the word Hebrews 12:5–11 uses.

a: rightness, justice and straight dealing
p: The book's goal is not cleverness alone: the three words describe right conduct toward others.
b: Tsedeq ('rightness, righteousness'), mishpat ('justice', fair judgment) and mesharim ('straightness, equity') are words of the law court and the covenant. Setting them in the purpose statement means that the 'good sense' Proverbs teaches is ethical: a wise person treats others rightly. The same three words return in 2:9, framing the father's first long speech. Ancient Egyptian instructions likewise joined success with ma'at, 'right order, justice' (see the note on 8:15).

a: the naive
p: The peti is not stupid but untaught, and can still be won by wisdom or by folly.
b: Peti comes from a root meaning 'be open, be enticed'. The naive person is the inexperienced young man who believes everything (14:15), and who can be led either way. That is why both Wisdom (1:22; 8:5; 9:4) and Woman Folly (9:16) address him with the same words. Older versions say 'the simple', as the Psalms on this site do (Psalm 19:7). The book is written for him: it means to give the naive 'shrewdness' before the gang or the strange woman gets to him.

a: shrewdness
p: The word for the serpent's craftiness in Genesis 3:1 is a virtue in Proverbs.
b: 'Ormah and the adjective 'arum mean practical cunning: seeing through a situation and acting to protect yourself. Elsewhere it is often bad: "the snake was shrewder than every wild animal" (Genesis 3:1), and a killer who acts with 'ormah gets no refuge (Exodus 21:14). Proverbs uses it as a skill the naive need (8:5, 12; 14:15; 22:3). The same is true of mezimmah, 'discretion', which can also mean 'scheme' (12:2; 24:8). The point: the same mental power can serve good or evil, and the young must learn to use it well.

a: the art of steering
p: Tachbulot is a sailor's word: the skill of pulling the ropes that steer a ship.
b: Tachbulot is related to chevel, 'rope', and to chovel, 'sailor' (Jonah 1:6; Ezekiel 27:8). The image is of guiding a ship by its lines. In Proverbs it means wise guidance, especially in hard decisions: war is made by steering, and many advisers bring victory (24:6; compare 11:14; 20:18). The verb 'acquire' (qanah, 'get, buy') is the same verb as in "Acquire wisdom" (4:5) and in 8:22.

a: a figure
p: The book expects work from its readers: some sayings are puzzles to be solved.
b: Hebrew melitsah appears only here and in Habakkuk 2:6, where it is a taunting figure of speech; it may mean an allusive or mocking saying that needs interpreting. Chidot are riddles, like Samson's (Judges 14:12–19) and the hard questions the queen of Sheba brought to Solomon (1 Kings 10:1). The verse promises that the book will teach its reader to decode such sayings. Some of the numerical sayings in chapter 30 and the paired sayings of 26:4–5 show what is meant.

a: The fear of the LORD
t: "The fear of the LORD" and "the LORD"
p: Not terror and not mere respect: awe before the God of Israel, shown in obedience.
b: Yir'at YHWH is the book's motto (1:7; 1:29; 2:5; 8:13; 9:10; 15:33; 31:30). The Plain keeps 'fear', because the Hebrew word is the ordinary word for being afraid, and the phrase includes a real sense of God's power to judge. But in use it means reverent awe that leads to obedience: "The fear of the LORD means hating evil" (8:13). It is closer to loyalty than to panic. 'The LORD' in small capitals stands for God's personal name, YHWH, which Jews do not pronounce and read as Adonai, 'Lord'. Its presence here matters: the wisdom Proverbs teaches is not general human cleverness but begins with the God of Israel.

a: where knowledge begins
t: Beginning, first step or best part?
p: Reshit can mean the start of something, its foundation, or its finest part. Each gives 1:7 a different sense.
b: Reshit means (1) the first in time, the starting point (Genesis 1:1, bereshit); (2) the first and best part, as with firstfruits (3:9; Exodus 23:19); (3) the chief or principal thing. Read the first way, the fear of the LORD is the first step, which you then leave behind as you learn more. Read the second or third way, it is the foundation and the core that stays under all knowledge. Most commentators think more than the first is meant, because the book keeps returning to the fear of the LORD as the goal as well as the start (2:5; 15:33). 9:10 uses a different word, techillah, 'start', so the book's two bookends say both: the fear of the LORD is where wisdom starts and what it amounts to. Psalm 111:10 and Job 28:28 give the same teaching.

a: Stubborn fools
p: Proverbs has several words for fools. The 'evil is the one who will not be taught.
b: Five kinds of fool walk through Proverbs. The peti is naive (1:4); the kesil is the dull, self-satisfied fool (1:22); the lets is the mocker (1:22); the nabal is the godless boor (17:7); and the 'evil, named here, is the fool who rejects correction: he thinks his own way is right (12:15), despises his father's discipline (15:5), and you could grind him in a mortar and his folly would not leave him (27:22). The Plain gives each its own English word throughout the book. The Hebrew order puts 'wisdom and discipline' first for emphasis, as the Plain's question does.

a: My son
t: Father and son, teacher and student
p: The speeches of 1–9 are cast as a father teaching his son, a form shared with Egyptian instructions.
b: Egyptian teachings were written as a father's words to his son: Ptahhotep, Any, Amenemope and the teaching for King Merikare all begin this way. In schools, 'father' and 'son' could also mean teacher and pupil (compare 2 Kings 2:12, where Elisha calls Elijah 'my father'). Some scholars therefore think Proverbs 1–9 was used to train young scribes or officials. Others point out that the mother is named beside the father (1:8; 6:20; compare 4:3; 31:1), which suggests a real household. Both settings may be in view: home teaching first, later used in schools. The 'son' is a young man about to marry and take his place in the town.

a: your mother's teaching
p: The word is torah, translated 'law' elsewhere on this site. Here it is a mother's instruction.
b: This site renders torah as 'law' (see Psalm 1:2). The word's root sense, though, is 'teaching, instruction', and in Proverbs a parent's or a sage's torah is plainly that (1:8; 3:1; 4:2; 6:20, 23; 7:2), as in Psalm 78:1. So the Plain says 'teaching' here. A mother as a teacher stands out: the Egyptian instructions are almost always from father to son, while Proverbs names the mother beside the father and ends with a mother's teaching to a king (31:1–9). Later Jewish readers heard more: Rashi takes 'your father' as God, who gave Moses the Torah, and reads 'your mother' (immekha) as 'your nation' (ummatekha), whose teaching is the sages' rulings that guard the Torah.

a: for nothing
p: The gang ambushes a man 'for nothing'; a few verses later the net is spread 'for nothing'.
b: Chinnam means 'for no reason, without cause, for free'. The gang plans to kill an innocent man 'for nothing', that is, though he has done nothing to them. In 1:17 the same word returns: the net is spread 'for nothing'. The repeat is a quiet joke at the gang's expense. They think they are hunters, but the trap they lay is really for themselves (1:18). The Plain uses 'for nothing' both times so the link can be heard.

a: the way Sheol does
p: The gang boasts that it is like the grave itself, an echo of the earth swallowing Korah's men alive.
b: Sheol, the world of the dead, is pictured with an open throat and an endless appetite (27:20; 30:16; Isaiah 5:14; Habakkuk 2:5). In Numbers 16:30–33 the earth opens its mouth and Korah's followers go down into Sheol alive. In Canaanite myth Death (Mot) is a devourer with jaws from earth to sky. The young men speak as if they were Death itself. 'The Pit' (bor, a cistern or deep hole) is a common poetic name for the grave (Psalm 28:1; Psalm 88:4).

a: For their feet race toward evil
t: A line shared with Isaiah and quoted by Paul
p: Isaiah 59:7 has almost the same words. Paul quotes them in Romans 3:15.
b: Isaiah 59:7 says of Judah's sinners that their feet run to evil and they hurry to shed innocent blood. Paul strings Isaiah 59:7–8 together with psalm verses in Romans 3:10–18 to show that all people are under sin, and his wording ("swift are their feet to shed blood") follows Isaiah's Greek. Whether Proverbs borrowed from Isaiah, Isaiah from a proverb, or both from a common saying is not known. The verse is missing from Codex Vaticanus and the first hand of Sinaiticus (see the variant).

a: For nothing the net is spread out
t: What does the bird proverb mean?
p: Three readings: the warned bird escapes, the bird is caught anyway, or the gang is caught in its own net.
b: The saying is short and its point is debated. (1) A bird that sees the net being spread will not fly into it, so a young man who has been warned should keep away (many moderns). (2) A bird sees the grain scattered on the net, thinks it is there for nothing, and goes down to eat; the gang is like that, blind to the trap they are building for themselves (Rashi; compare Fox). (3) The net that is 'spread for nothing' is the gang's ambush of the innocent, and it is the gang that will be caught (1:18). Reading 2 fits 1:18 best: the men set a trap for blood and it turns out to be their own. 'Every winged thing' is literally 'every owner of a wing'.

a: grab at crooked gain
p: Botsea' is profit taken by force or fraud, a 'cut' of what belongs to others.
b: The Hebrew says literally 'everyone who cuts a cut' (botsea' batsa'): the word first meant to cut off a piece, then to take an illegal profit. It is the bribe-taking of Samuel's sons (1 Samuel 8:3) and the greed of Jeremiah's leaders (Jeremiah 6:13). The closing line, 'it robs its owners of their life', turns the gang's plan around: they meant to take the lives of others for profit, but the profit takes theirs.

a: Wisdom
p: For the first time, wisdom is a woman who speaks in public like a prophet.
b: Here wisdom becomes a person, a woman who shouts in the streets and the gates, where business, law and gossip happened. She will speak again in 8:1–36 and invite guests to her house in 9:1–6, and she has a rival, Woman Folly (9:13–18). The Hebrew form here is chokmot, an unusual plural, probably a plural of majesty ('great Wisdom') as in 9:1; the verb is singular. Who is she? The poet's picture of God's own wisdom; a teacher's figure for the book's teaching; a reworking of an Egyptian goddess like Ma'at or of a Canaanite goddess; later Jewish readers say the Torah, and Christian readers the Word of God. See the chapter page and 8:22–31.

a: above the noisy crowds
p: The Hebrew says 'at the head of the noisy (places)'; the Greek read 'at the top of the walls'.
b: The Hebrew homiyyot, 'noisy ones', is an unusual way to name busy streets, which is what most translations make of it. The Greek has 'on the top of the walls', which reflects chomot, 'walls', a word that differs by one letter. Either way, she stands where the most people will hear her: on the walls above the gate or in the loudest part of the town. The city gate was the town's courthouse, market and meeting place (Ruth 4:1–11; 31:23).

a: mockers
p: The lets is the scoffer who sneers at correction and teaches others to sneer.
b: Lets and its verb describe a person who makes fun of what is serious, refuses rebuke (9:7–8; 13:1; 15:12) and stirs up trouble (22:10; 29:8). Proverbs says that this is his very name (21:24). He is beyond the reach of teaching, unlike the naive. The same word appears in the first verse of the Psalms (Psalm 1:1, 'where mockers sit'). Wisdom's three addressees here, naive, mockers and fools, run from those who can still be taught to those who will not be.

a: I will pour out my spirit to you
p: Wisdom speaks like God in the prophets, promising to pour out her spirit and words.
b: Ruach means 'spirit, breath, wind'. Here it may mean Wisdom's thoughts or breath, which come out as words (the next line). But the phrase 'pour out my spirit' is the language of God's promise in Isaiah 44:3, Ezekiel 39:29 and Joel 2:28, which Peter quotes at Pentecost (Acts 2:17). Christian readers have heard in Wisdom's offer a hint of the Spirit's gift; most commentators read it as Wisdom's teaching poured out freely for anyone who turns. Either way, the offer is conditional: 'turn back when I rebuke you'.

a: Since I called and you said no
p: Her speech borrows the words of Jeremiah and Isaiah: God called, the people refused, so he will not answer.
b: "I called, and you did not answer" is a prophetic charge against Israel (Isaiah 65:12; Isaiah 66:4; Jeremiah 7:13). The prophets also warn that those who ignore God will cry out in disaster and not be heard (Micah 3:4; Jeremiah 11:11; Hosea 5:6). Wisdom takes up this language as if she spoke for God. Many scholars see this as a sign that the speech was written when prophecy and wisdom were being drawn together, perhaps after the exile. It also means that rejecting wisdom is not just foolish; it is rejecting God (1:29).
r: Isaiah 65:12; Isaiah 66:4; Jeremiah 7:13; Jeremiah 7:24–27; Micah 3:4; Hosea 5:6; Zechariah 7:13; 1:29

a: laugh at your disaster
p: Wisdom's laughter shocks many readers. It echoes God laughing at the rebels in Psalm 2.
b: God laughs at the nations who plot against him (Psalm 2:4; Psalm 37:13; Psalm 59:8). Wisdom's laugh is of that kind: not cruelty but the certainty that rebellion will collapse on itself. Some commentators stress that the laughter is a teacher's warning, spoken while there is still time, in order to make the hearer turn (1:23). Others hold that the speech means exactly what it says: there is a point past which refusal cannot be undone. The verse is about consequences that come 'like devastation', not about God taking pleasure in pain (compare Ezekiel 18:23).

a: Then they will call me
p: Wisdom stops speaking to the hearers and talks about them, as if they were already gone.
b: Up to 1:27 Wisdom says 'you'. In 1:28–32 she says 'they'. The change is common in Hebrew poetry, but here it has force: she turns away from those who would not listen, and speaks about them to whoever is still listening. Then in 1:33 she turns to the one who does listen.

a: Turning away
p: Meshuvah is Jeremiah's word for Israel's faithlessness.
b: Meshuvah comes from shuv, 'turn', the same root as 'Turn back' in 1:23. Wisdom asked them to turn toward her; instead they turned away. Jeremiah uses the noun for Israel's backsliding (Jeremiah 2:19; Jeremiah 3:22; Jeremiah 14:7). The other killer is shalvah, 'ease, being carefree': fools die of complacency.

a: My son, if you take in my words
t: One long sentence, shaped like an alphabet
p: Chapter 2 is a single sentence of 22 verses, the number of letters in the Hebrew alphabet.
b: The whole chapter is one 'if... then' sentence: if you seek wisdom (2:1–4), then you will find the LORD's knowledge (2:5–8) and understand what is right (2:9–11), and wisdom will rescue you from the evil man (2:12–15) and the strange woman (2:16–19), so that you walk with the good (2:20–22). It has 22 verses, like the alphabet acrostics, though it is not an acrostic. Scholars have noticed that the first half is led by words beginning with alef, the first letter ('im 'if', 'az 'then'), and the second half by words beginning with lamed, the letter that begins the second half of the alphabet (lehatsilkha, 'to rescue you'). The chapter reads like a table of contents for chapters 3–7.

a: the way people hunt for silver
p: The search for wisdom is compared to mining, as in Job 28.
b: Silver and 'buried treasure' (matmonim, things hidden in the ground) picture the hard labor of mining. Job 28 describes miners cutting shafts in the rock for silver and gold, and then asks, "But wisdom: where can it be found?" (Job 28:12). Proverbs agrees that wisdom is worth more than metal (3:14; 8:10–11) but is more hopeful than Job: whoever searches will find (2:5; 8:17). Jesus' parable of the treasure hidden in a field (Matthew 13:44) uses the same picture for the kingdom of God.

a: the knowledge of God
p: In Hebrew, 'knowing' God means a relationship of loyalty, not only facts about him.
b: Da'at Elohim is a phrase of the prophet Hosea: "there is no faithfulness, no loyal love, no knowledge of God in the land" (Hosea 4:1; compare Hosea 6:6). It means knowing God as a covenant partner, which shows itself in how one lives. 'God' (Elohim) is rare in Proverbs, which nearly always says 'the LORD'; in chapters 1–9 it appears only here, in 2:17 and in 3:4 (elsewhere 25:2 and 30:9; 30:5 has Eloah). The two lines of the verse make 'the fear of the LORD' and 'the knowledge of God' one thing.

a: knowledge and understanding come out of his mouth
p: Wisdom is sought by hard effort, and yet it is given by God. Proverbs holds both together.
b: 2:1–4 says the young man must search; 2:6 says the LORD gives. Proverbs does not see a conflict: the search is how one receives the gift. Solomon received wisdom by asking for it (1 Kings 3:9–12). James 1:5 tells anyone who lacks wisdom to ask God, who gives generously. Wisdom that comes 'out of his mouth' is close to the idea of God's word (Psalm 33:6; Sirach 24:3, where Wisdom says she came out of the mouth of the Most High).

a: sound wisdom
p: Tushiyyah means wisdom that works: good sense that brings success.
b: Tushiyyah appears mainly in Job and Proverbs (2:7; 3:21; 8:14; 18:1; Job 5:12; Job 6:13; Job 11:6). Its range runs from 'competence, success' to 'resourcefulness, sound wisdom'. The Plain follows Job's 'sound wisdom' on this site. Here the LORD 'stores it up' for the upright like a treasure in a storeroom, matching the treasure of 2:4.

a: whose talk is upside down
p: Tahpukhot is perversity: words that turn the truth on its head.
b: Tahpukhot comes from haphakh, 'turn over', the verb for overturning Sodom (Genesis 19:25). The noun is almost limited to Proverbs (2:12, 14; 6:14; 8:13; 10:31–32; 16:28, 30; 23:33) and names speech or schemes that reverse right and wrong. Older English said 'froward'. The Plain says 'upside down' so that the root picture stays visible each time it returns.

a: the strange woman
p: She appears in chapters 2, 5, 6, 7 and 22–23. Is she an adulteress, a foreigner, or a figure for folly?
b: Hebrew zarah is the feminine of zar, 'outsider', someone outside one's family, priesthood or people. Nokhriyyah is the feminine of nokhri, 'foreigner' (as Ruth calls herself, Ruth 2:10). Five readings: (1) Another man's wife, 'strange' because she is outside your own marriage; 2:17, 6:26–35 and 7:19 make her married, and this is the view of most commentators (Fox, Waltke). (2) A woman of another people, as in Solomon's 'foreign women' (1 Kings 11:1) and the mixed marriages of Ezra 10; some link the chapters to that crisis (Blenkinsopp, Washington). (3) A woman tied to a foreign cult (Boström; see 7:14). (4) A personification of Folly, the dark twin of Lady Wisdom (9:13–18), and so of any false teaching; the Greek, the Qumran poem 4Q184 and later Jewish readers who saw heresy in her took this line. (5) A combination: a real danger that the poet makes into a symbol. See the chapter page.

a: whose words are smooth
p: Her danger is in her speech: the verb means 'make slippery', the flattery of 5:3 and 7:21.
b: Hecheliqah, 'she makes smooth', is the language of flattery (Psalm 5:9; Psalm 12:2). In chapters 5 and 7 the woman's seduction is almost all words: honey on her lips (5:3), a long speech (7:14–20) and 'her much persuading' (7:21). The father's lesson is about listening: which voice will a young man trust, the father's and Wisdom's or hers?

a: the close friend she had when she was young
p: Alluf is 'close friend, companion'; here it is her husband, and 'the covenant of her God' is probably her marriage.
b: Alluf ne'ureha, 'the companion of her youth', is the husband she married young; Jeremiah uses the same phrase of God as Israel's husband (Jeremiah 3:4). 'The covenant of her God' may be the marriage covenant made before God, as in Malachi 2:14 ('the wife of your youth... your wife by covenant'), or Israel's covenant at Sinai, whose commandments forbid adultery (Exodus 20:14). Either way, she is an Israelite who has broken a sacred bond, which supports the view that the 'strange woman' is an adulteress. The Greek makes her 'evil counsel' that forsakes 'the teaching of youth' and 'the divine covenant'.
orig: אלוף נעוריה (alluf ne'ureha); ברית אלהיה (berit eloheha)

a: her house is sinking down to death
p: The verb 'sinks' is feminine, but 'house' is masculine. The text may be slightly damaged.
b: Shachah el mavet betah: the verb shachah is feminine, while bayit, 'house', is masculine. Suggested solutions: read netivatah, 'her path', for 'her house' (compare 7:27); take the woman as subject ('she sinks down to death; her house...'); or revocalize the verb. The meaning is clear whatever the grammar: going into her house is going down to death. 'The shades' (refa'im) are the dead, ghostly residents of Sheol (9:18; Psalm 88:10; Isaiah 14:9).
orig: שחה אל מות ביתה (shachah el mavet betah)

a: All who go in to her never return
p: The Hebrew phrase is the usual idiom for sex. Its double sense: they enter her house and never come out.
b: Ba' el, 'go in to', is the Bible's ordinary phrase for sleeping with a woman (Genesis 16:2; Genesis 38:16; 6:29). Here it also means entering her house, which leads to death (2:18). 'They never return' recalls the description of the land of the dead as a place of no return (Job 7:9–10; Job 10:21), a phrase also known from Mesopotamian poems about the underworld.

a: The land will be home for upright people
t: Who will live in the land?
p: The promise of the land, from Deuteronomy and the Psalms, becomes the reward of the upright.
b: Deuteronomy ties life in the land to keeping the covenant (Deuteronomy 4:1; Deuteronomy 16:20). Psalm 37 repeats that the wicked will be cut off while "the humble will take possession of the land" (Psalm 37:11). Proverbs uses the same promise for individuals (10:30). Jesus' saying that the meek will inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5) echoes Psalm 37:11. Readers who date Proverbs 1–9 after the exile hear in 2:21–22 a hope about who will be allowed to stay in Judah.
r: Deuteronomy 4:1; Deuteronomy 16:20; Psalm 37:9; Psalm 37:11; Psalm 37:29; 10:30; Matthew 5:5

a: my teaching: do not forget it
p: Chapter 3 borrows the words of Deuteronomy: don't forget, keep the commands, tie them on, write them on the heart.
b: Deuteronomy warns Israel not to forget the LORD and his commands (Deuteronomy 4:9; Deuteronomy 8:11), promises long life for keeping them (Deuteronomy 5:33; Deuteronomy 6:2), and says to tie them on the hand and write them on the doorposts (Deuteronomy 6:8–9; Deuteronomy 11:18–20). Proverbs 3:1–4, 6:20–23 and 7:1–3 use the same pattern for a father's teaching. Scholars debate what this means: the sages may be presenting their teaching as an echo of the Torah, or both may draw on a common teaching style. Jewish readers have long taken the father's 'teaching' as the Torah itself.

a: loyal love and faithfulness
p: The pair that describes God at Sinai is here a virtue the son must wear.
b: Chesed ve'emet, 'loyal love and faithfulness', is the LORD's character in Exodus 34:6, "great in loyal love and faithfulness". In Proverbs the pair describes human loyalty and reliability (14:22; 16:6; 20:28). 'Tie them around your neck' may mean wearing them like a charm or a seal; 'write them on your heart's tablet' recalls the new covenant promise of Jeremiah 31:33 and Paul's 'letter written on tablets of human hearts' (2 Corinthians 3:3).

a: in the eyes of God and of people
p: Said of young Samuel and of the boy Jesus. Paul quotes the Greek of this verse.
b: The phrase describes the growing Samuel (1 Samuel 2:26) and the twelve-year-old Jesus, who grew "in favor with God and with people" (Luke 2:52). The Greek of 3:4 reads differently: 'and take thought for what is good before the Lord and people'. Paul uses that Greek wording twice: give thought to what is good in the sight of all (Romans 12:17) and 'we plan what is right, not only before the Lord but also before people' (2 Corinthians 8:21).

a: do not lean on what you yourself understand
p: The verse does not reject thinking. It rejects relying on your own insight in place of God.
b: The verb sha'an means to put your weight on something, as on a staff or a wall (2 Kings 18:21; Isaiah 10:20). Proverbs prizes understanding everywhere (2:2–3; 4:5, 7), so the warning is about self-reliance: making your own judgment the thing you lean on instead of the LORD. The next verses spell this out: 'Do not be wise in your own eyes' (3:7; compare 26:12 and 28:26). Christian readers often take 3:5–6 as a call to faith in daily decisions. Rashi reads it as 'spend your money to find a teacher, and do not rely on your own understanding'; Gersonides (Ralbag) warns that whoever credits his success to his own cleverness forfeits the help of God's providence. The Greek says, 'do not be lifted up by your own wisdom'.
orig: ואל בינתך אל תשען (ve'el binatekha al tisha'en)

a: Know him on every road you take
p: The Hebrew is simply 'know him'. 'Acknowledge' or 'submit to' are interpretations.
b: Da'ehu means 'know him': be aware of him, keep him in mind, stay in relationship with him, in every part of life (compare 2:5, 'the knowledge of God'). 'He will level your paths' (yeyasher) means he will make them straight and smooth, free of obstacles, the picture of Isaiah 40:3–4. It promises a life that reaches its goal, not a life without trouble; the same verb is used of upright conduct in 11:5 and 15:21.

a: Do not be wise in your own eyes.
p: A Hebrew idiom that returns in 26:12 and 28:11, and a warning Isaiah and Paul repeat.
b: The Hebrew idiom 'wise in your own eyes' means trusting your own opinion of yourself. Isaiah 5:21 pronounces woe on those who are wise in their own eyes, and Paul tells the Romans, "Do not become wise in your own opinion" (Romans 12:16). The cure in Proverbs is the fear of the LORD and turning from evil, the same pairing as Job 1:1 and Job 28:28.

a: navel
p: The Hebrew says 'navel'. The Greek has 'body', and some scholars correct the Hebrew to 'flesh'.
b: Shor is the navel or the umbilical cord (Ezekiel 16:4; Song of Songs 7:2). It may stand for the body's center, so 'healing for your navel' means health to your whole self, with 'bones' as the inner frame. The Greek has 'body', and many scholars read she'er, 'flesh', with one letter changed, which would match 4:22, 'healing for all their flesh'. The Plain keeps the Hebrew image. 'A drink for your bones' (shiqquy, moisture) pictures bones kept moist and alive, unlike the 'dried-up bones' of 17:22.

a: the first share of everything you harvest
p: The only call to give an offering in Proverbs 1–9, with a promise of full barns.
b: Israel gave the first of its harvest to the LORD (Exodus 23:19; Deuteronomy 26:1–11). Proverbs links that gift with abundance (3:10), as Malachi 3:10 does with the tithe. Readers differ on how to take such promises. Many see them as the normal pattern of God's world, not a guarantee in every case, since Proverbs itself knows that the righteous can be poor (15:16; 16:8; 28:6) and Job and Ecclesiastes question any simple rule. Some Christian teachers, especially in 'prosperity' preaching, read 3:9–10 as a promise of wealth for those who give; most Jewish and Christian commentators reject that as a misreading of the genre, in which sayings state what usually happens.

a: The LORD's discipline, my son, do not reject
p: Hebrews 12:5–6 quotes 3:11–12 from the Greek to encourage Christians under persecution.
b: Hebrews reminds its readers of the exhortation that speaks to them 'as sons' and quotes these verses: "My son, do not think little of the Lord's discipline, and do not give up when he rebukes you. For whoever the Lord loves, he disciplines, and he whips every son he takes in" (Hebrews 12:5–6). The writer then argues that hardship proves they are God's children, since every father disciplines his sons (Hebrews 12:7–11). The quotation follows the Greek, which reads the last line differently from the Hebrew (see the variant on 3:12). Revelation 3:19 echoes the verse: "I correct and train everyone I love". Eliphaz says the same to Job (Job 5:17).

a: the way a father treats the son he takes pleasure in
p: Jews and Christians both read these verses as a key to suffering: hardship can be God's loving correction.
b: Proverbs means first the father's discipline of his son, which the book's readers would have known as both words and blows (13:24). It applies that to God. In the Talmud, the rabbis speak of yissurin shel ahavah, 'sufferings of love', and cite this verse: when suffering comes and a person finds no sin to explain it, it may be God's love (Bavli Berakhot 5a). Christian readers, following Hebrews 12, take hardship as training for holiness. Both traditions also warn against using the verse to tell a sufferer that pain must be deserved, which is the mistake of Job's friends (Job 42:7).

a: Happy
p: Ashrei, often 'blessed', means fortunate, well off: the opening word of Psalm 1.
b: Ashrei begins and me'ushshar ends the poem of 3:13–18, a frame of happiness around the praise of Wisdom. The word describes the good condition of a person, not a blessing given by someone (that is barukh). Psalm 1:1 begins the same way. 'Draws out understanding' uses yafiq, 'bring out, obtain', the verb of 8:35, 'he draws favor from the LORD'.

a: red coral
p: Peninim were costly red stones or corals; 'rubies' and 'pearls' are guesses.
b: Peninim are always a symbol of great value (8:11; 20:15; 31:10; Job 28:18). Lamentations 4:7 says that Jerusalem's princes were 'redder than peninim', which points to red coral, prized in the ancient Mediterranean world. The KJV's 'rubies' fits the color; 'pearls', from rabbinic Hebrew, does not. The Greek has 'costly stones' and adds two lines: 'No evil will stand against her; she is well known to all who come near her.'

a: She holds length of days in her right hand
t: Wisdom and the Egyptian goddess Ma'at
p: Egyptian art shows Ma'at, 'Right Order', holding the sign of life in one hand and a scepter in the other.
b: Christa Kayatz pointed out that Egyptian images of Ma'at, goddess of truth, justice and cosmic order, show her holding the ankh (the sign of life) and a scepter (power and wealth), and that Ma'at was said to be loved by the gods and present at creation. Lady Wisdom with long life in one hand and wealth and honor in the other, and Wisdom beside God at creation (8:22–31), may borrow this picture. The link is real but limited: Ma'at was a goddess, while Wisdom in Proverbs is the LORD's creature or attribute. The Greek adds: 'From her mouth comes righteousness; she carries law and mercy on her tongue.'

a: a tree of life
t: "She is a tree of life" in the synagogue
p: This verse is sung as the Torah scroll is returned to the ark; the scroll's wooden rollers are called 'trees of life'.
b: The tree of life stood in Eden (Genesis 2:9) and was closed to humans after the fall (Genesis 3:22–24). Proverbs uses the image four times (3:18; 11:30; 13:12; 15:4) for what restores life. Jewish tradition identifies Wisdom here with the Torah: in the synagogue service, when the scroll is put back in the ark, the congregation sings Etz chayyim hi, 'She is a tree of life to those who hold her fast', followed by 3:17. The wooden rollers of the scroll are called atsei chayyim. Christian readers connect the tree with the cross and with the tree of life in the new Jerusalem (Revelation 22:2).

a: It was by wisdom that the LORD founded the earth
p: A short preview of 8:22–31, repeated almost word for word in Jeremiah.
b: Jeremiah 10:12 and Jeremiah 51:15 say that God made the earth by his power, founded the world by his wisdom and stretched out the heavens by his understanding. Psalm 104:24 says, "You made every one of them with wisdom." Here wisdom is God's skill, the tool he used. In 8:22–31 Wisdom herself will speak as one who was there. 'The deeps burst open' (3:20) may refer to the springs that water the earth (Genesis 7:11) or to the dividing of the waters at creation (Genesis 1:6–9).
r: Jeremiah 10:12; Jeremiah 51:15; Psalm 104:24; 8:22–31; Genesis 1:6–9; Genesis 7:11; Job 38:4–11

a: the one you rely on
p: Kesel can mean 'confidence' or 'loins, side'. The LORD is either your trust or at your side.
b: Kesel means 'loins' (Leviticus 3:4), 'confidence' (Job 8:14; Psalm 78:7) and, in a bad sense, 'foolishness' (Ecclesiastes 7:25). 'The LORD will be your confidence' is the usual reading. Some prefer 'the LORD will be at your side', from the sense 'flank'. The two lines together say that the LORD keeps the one who trusts him from the trap.

a: Do not keep good from its owners
p: Literally 'its owners': those to whom the good is due. The Greek says 'the needy'.
b: Be'alav, 'its masters', may mean those who have a right to it: a worker owed wages that day (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14–15), a lender owed repayment, or a neighbor owed a returned pledge. The Greek and many readers widen it to the poor, whose need gives them a claim on those who can help. Jewish law's rule that a hired worker is paid the same day (Mishnah, tractate Bava Metzia, chapter 9, applying Leviticus 19:13) works in the same spirit. James 2:15–16 makes the same point about warm words without help. Hebrew 'your hand' is 'your hands' in the written text (Ketiv); the sense is the same.
orig: אל תמנע טוב מבעליו (al timna' tov mibbe'alav)

a: tomorrow I'll give it to you
p: The Greek adds 'for you do not know what tomorrow will bring', a line also found in 27:1.
b: Putting off a neighbor with 'tomorrow' is a way of refusing while seeming to agree. The Greek adds the reason not to delay: you do not know what the next day will bring, words close to 27:1. James 4:13–14 warns those who plan for tomorrow, 'you do not know what your life will be like tomorrow'.

a: plow up trouble
p: The verb charash means both 'plow' and 'devise': scheming is pictured as plowing.
b: Charash is the farmer's verb for plowing and the craftsman's for engraving, and from that it came to mean planning, usually planning evil (6:14, 18; 12:20; 14:22). The Plain keeps the farm picture: the schemer plows up harm the way a farmer turns the soil before sowing. Hosea 10:13 says, 'You have plowed wickedness; you have reaped injustice.'

a: with the upright he shares his secrets
p: Sod is a close circle of advisers, or the secrets shared within it.
b: Sod is a council or a confidential conversation (15:22; Jeremiah 23:18, 'who has stood in the LORD's council?'; Amos 3:7). The upright are God's intimates; the devious (naloz, the twisting word of 2:15) are 'something abhorrent'. Psalm 25:14 uses the same phrase: "The LORD shares his secrets with those who fear him". Jesus tells his disciples he calls them friends, not slaves, because he has told them everything (John 15:15).

a: Mockers he mocks
p: James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5 quote the Greek: 'God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.'
b: The Hebrew is a play on words: with mockers God is a mocker (hu yalits), turning their scorn back on them (compare Psalm 18:26). The Greek turns it into a general rule: 'The Lord resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.' Both James (4:6) and 1 Peter (5:5) quote that Greek wording, with 'God' for 'the Lord': James to warn quarreling Christians against friendship with the world, Peter to tell young and old to clothe themselves with humility. Mary's song makes the same reversal (Luke 1:51–53). Whether the second line means the 'humble' or the 'afflicted' depends on a Ketiv and Qere (see the variant).

a: fools carry away disgrace
p: The Hebrew may mean fools 'raise up disgrace' or that disgrace 'lifts up' fools for all to see.
b: Merim qalon is literally 'lifting up disgrace'. Suggestions: fools 'carry off' disgrace as their share (contrasting with the wise who 'inherit' honor); disgrace 'exalts' fools, that is, makes them conspicuous, a bitter irony; or, with a small change, fools 'inherit' disgrace. The Greek has 'the ungodly exalt dishonor'. The contrast is clear: honor for the wise, shame for fools.

a: Sons
p: Here and in 5:7, 7:24 and 8:32 the teacher speaks to 'sons' in the plural, as to a class.
b: Most of chapters 1–7 say 'my son', singular, the voice of a father at home. The plural banim here, with 'a father' rather than 'your father', sounds more like a teacher with pupils; Egyptian instructions likewise move between a real son and a scribe's students. Many scholars take this as a sign that household teaching and school teaching had merged by the time the book was written. Others hear a real father passing on to all his children what his own father taught him (4:3–4).

a: What I hand you is good learning
p: The Mishnah reads this verse as God speaking: the Torah is the good thing he gave to Israel.
b: Leqach tov, 'good learning', is what one 'takes' or receives. Rabbi Akiva says in the Mishnah: 'Beloved are Israel, for a precious instrument was given to them, the instrument by which the world was created', and proves it from this verse, reading 'my teaching' (torati) as God's Torah (Mishnah Avot 3:14). The same verse closes the Torah service in many synagogues, sung as the scroll is returned to the ark. The father's 'teaching' has become the LORD's.

a: young and tender, the only one my mother had
p: Chronicles calls Solomon 'tender', so Jewish readers heard Solomon recalling David's teaching.
b: David calls Solomon 'young and tender' (na'ar varakh) in 1 Chronicles 22:5 and 29:1, with the same word rakh, 'tender', as here. Rashi and others read 4:3–9 as Solomon quoting his father David. 'The only one' (yachid) cannot be literal for Solomon, since Bathsheba bore four sons (1 Chronicles 3:5); it means 'the dearly loved one', as Isaac is Abraham's yachid (Genesis 22:2). Whatever the original speaker, the picture is of wisdom handed down through three generations: grandfather, father, son.

a: Acquire wisdom; acquire understanding.
p: Qanah means 'get, acquire', often by buying. Wisdom is a purchase worth everything you own.
b: The verb qanah is used for buying land and goods (Genesis 47:20; Ruth 4:9) and for acquiring in general. The father's command is commercial: get wisdom as you would buy a field, and pay whatever it costs (4:7; compare 23:23, 'Buy truth, and do not sell it'). The same verb returns in 8:22, where Wisdom says that the LORD 'acquired' her before his works. The Plain keeps 'acquire' in 1:5, 4:5, 4:7 and 8:22 so that the link can be seen; elsewhere in the book the same verb is rendered 'gaining' (16:16), 'the price of' (17:16) and 'buy' (23:23). See the note on 8:22.

a: Where wisdom starts: acquire wisdom!
t: The start of wisdom is getting it
p: A riddle-like line: the first step toward wisdom is simply to decide to get it.
b: Reshit chokhmah qeneh chokhmah can be read 'The beginning of wisdom is: acquire wisdom', or 'The best thing is wisdom: acquire wisdom'. On the first reading the verse is a paradox: you cannot start until you want it badly enough to pay for it. 1:7 and 9:10 say that the fear of the LORD is the beginning; this verse adds the human side, the will to seek. The verse is missing from the main Greek manuscripts (see the variant).
orig: ראשית חכמה קנה חכמה (reshit chokhmah qeneh chokhmah)

a: hold her close
p: Prize her, hold her close, and she will crown you: the language of courtship.
b: The father speaks of wisdom as a woman to be loved (4:6) and embraced (techabbeqennah, 'you hold her close'), who honors the man who holds her and sets a wreath on his head (4:9). 'Hold her high' renders a rare verb (salseleha), perhaps 'cherish' or 'heap up a mound for her'. The courtship language prepares for the contrast of chapters 5–7: a young man will embrace someone, and it should be Wisdom and the wife of his youth (5:18–20), not the strange woman. The Wisdom of Solomon takes the image further: 'I loved her and sought her from my youth, and desired to take her for my bride' (Wisdom of Solomon 8:2).
r: 4:6; 4:9; 5:20; 7:4; Wisdom of Solomon 8:2; Song of Songs 3:11

a: In wisdom's road I have trained you
p: Chapter 4 sets out the image that governs the whole book: two roads, one of light and one of darkness.
b: Road words fill chapters 1–9: derekh 'road', orach 'path', ma'gal 'track', netivah 'lane'. 4:10–19 sets the straight road of wisdom (4:11–13) against the path of the wicked (4:14–17) and ends with a picture: one road grows brighter like the dawn, the other is black as night (4:18–19). The same choice appears in Psalm 1, Deuteronomy 30:15–20 and Jeremiah 21:8; Jesus speaks of the narrow and the wide gate (Matthew 7:13–14), and the early Christian Didache opens: 'There are two ways, one of life and one of death.'

a: They do not sleep if they have done no harm
p: The wicked cannot rest until they have done harm, as a righteous person cannot rest until a duty is done.
b: The picture is of people for whom evil is a craving: they lose sleep over a day without it, and their food and drink are wickedness and violence (4:17). Compare the wicked man who plots evil on his bed (Psalm 36:4; Micah 2:1). The Hebrew of the second line has a Ketiv/Qere difference: the written text has 'until they stumble', and the text read aloud has 'until they make someone stumble' (see the variant).
orig: לא ישנו אם לא ירעו (lo yishnu im lo yare'u)

a: like the first gleam of morning
p: The road of the righteous is like daybreak that grows to full noon.
b: Or nogah is the first light before sunrise (2 Samuel 23:4; Isaiah 60:3); the light 'goes on and grows brighter' (holekh va'or) 'until the day is firm' (ad nekhon hayyom), probably high noon. The image is of growth: a good life becomes clearer as it goes. The contrast in 4:19 is total darkness, in which people trip without knowing why. Judges 5:31 likewise compares those who love the LORD to the sun rising in its strength.
orig: כאור נגה (ke'or nogah); עד נכון היום (ad nekhon hayyom)

a: watch over your heart
p: In Hebrew the heart is the mind and will, not only the feelings.
b: Lev is the center of thought, choice and desire: people 'say in their heart' what they think (Psalm 14:1), and 'senseless' in Proverbs is 'lacking heart' (6:32). 'More than anything you keep watch over' (mikkol mishmar) may also mean 'with all vigilance'. The second line gives the reason: the heart is the source of the 'outgoings' of life (totse'ot, a word for a river's sources or a boundary's ends). Jesus says the same of evil: out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery and theft (Mark 7:21–23).
orig: מכל משמר נצר לבך (mikkol mishmar netsor libbekha)

a: a crooked mouth
p: After the heart come the mouth, the eyes and the feet: the whole body is to be kept straight.
b: 4:23–27 moves through the body: heart (4:23), mouth and lips (4:24), eyes and eyelids (4:25) and feet (4:26–27). 'Iqqeshut peh is 'twistedness of mouth', speech that bends the truth (compare 6:12). The list matches the parts of the body that the LORD hates when they are misused in 6:16–19.

a: Level the track your foot walks on
p: Hebrews 12:13 quotes the Greek of this verse: 'make straight paths for your feet'.
b: The Hebrew verb palles means 'make level' or 'weigh, survey' (5:6, 21). The Greek has 'Make straight tracks for your feet', and Hebrews 12:12–13 uses those words right after quoting Proverbs 3:11–12 on discipline: strengthen your weak knees and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may be healed. The writer of Hebrews read Proverbs 3 and 4 together, as one teaching on perseverance.

a: Do not veer off to the right or the left
p: A phrase from Deuteronomy and Joshua for keeping the commandments exactly.
b: Moses tells Israel not to turn aside 'to the right or to the left' from what the LORD commanded (Deuteronomy 5:32; Deuteronomy 28:14), and the LORD says the same to Joshua about the book of the law (Joshua 1:7). The father applies the covenant phrase to his own teaching. The Greek adds two verses explaining that God knows the ways on the right, while those on the left are crooked (see the variant).

a: Honey drips from the strange woman's lips
p: Her kisses and her words are sweet and smooth; the same images praise the bride in the Song of Songs.
b: Nofet is honey dripping from the comb, and the 'palate' (chek) is the mouth as the organ of taste and of speech. In the Song of Songs the lover says, 'Your lips drip honey, my bride' (Song of Songs 4:11), so the imagery itself is not evil: it is love's language used outside its place. Her smooth palate recalls her 'smooth words' (2:16; 7:5, 21). The Greek adds a first line, 'Pay no attention to a worthless woman', and calls her 'a prostitute'.
orig: נפת תטפנה שפתי זרה (nofet tittofnah siftei zarah)

a: bitter as wormwood
p: Sweet at first, bitter at the end: the contrast between 5:3 and 5:4 is the lesson of the chapter.
b: Wormwood (la'anah) is a bitter desert plant, used in the Bible for the taste of injustice and judgment (Amos 5:7; Lamentations 3:15, 19; compare Revelation 8:11). 'What she leads to at last' is literally 'her end' (acharitah): Proverbs often judges a thing by where it ends (14:12; 23:32). A 'sword that cuts both ways' is literally a 'sword of mouths' (cherev pifiyyot), a pun on her mouth in 5:3. Hebrews 4:12 uses the same image of God's word.

a: She never takes the level road of life
p: The Hebrew of this verse is unusual; translators differ over whether she or the young man is the subject.
b: The verse begins with pen, usually 'lest', and the verb can be 'she' or 'you' ('lest you weigh the path of life'). Most modern translations take it as 'she does not keep to the path of life', as the Plain does; the King James Version has 'Lest thou shouldest ponder the path of life'. The Greek reads 'for she does not walk the roads of life'. The second line says her tracks 'wander' (na'u, the word for a drunkard's staggering) and she does not even know it: she is lost herself, not only a danger to others.
orig: ארח חיים פן תפלס (orach chayyim pen tefalles)

a: So now, sons, listen to me
p: This exact call to 'sons' returns in 7:24 and 8:32, each time at a turning point.
b: Ve'attah vanim shim'u li, 'So now, sons, listen to me', stands at the turn from description to command here, at the end of the story of chapter 7 (7:24), and in Wisdom's own mouth at the end of her speech (8:32). The repeated line makes Wisdom's voice and the father's voice the same voice. The Plain gives the three the same wording.
orig: ועתה בנים שמעו לי (ve'attah vanim shim'u li)

a: your years to a cruel man
p: The father lists what the affair will take: honor, years, strength and money. Who the 'cruel man' is is debated.
b: 5:9–10 speak of losing 'splendor' (hod, honor or vigor) to others, years to a 'cruel man' (akhzari), and wealth and labor to 'outsiders' and a 'foreigner's house'. Readers suggest: (1) the woman's husband, who will demand compensation or revenge (6:34–35); (2) the community that punishes the adulterer; (3) the woman's people, if she is a foreigner, who will absorb his estate; or (4) no one in particular: the point is that what a man built for his own family goes to strangers. The verses read like a warning about inheritance and household wealth as much as about sin.

a: in the middle of the assembly and the community
p: The ruined man says he came close to disaster before the whole community. This may mean a public trial.
b: Qahal and 'edah are the words for Israel gathered as a body, used in the Torah for the people that judges and punishes (Numbers 35:24; Leviticus 24:14). The law prescribed death for adultery with a married woman (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22), so the man may mean he nearly faced execution. Or he may mean only that he was shamed in public (6:33). Either way, the private sin ends as public ruin. His speech (5:12–14) is a confession in the style of a lament, too late.

a: Drink the water your own cistern holds
p: Cistern, well and spring are images for a man's own wife and the joy of their love.
b: In a dry land, a private cistern (bor) or well (be'er) was precious property. The Song of Songs calls the bride 'a garden locked, a spring sealed' and 'a well of living water' (Song of Songs 4:12, 15). The father tells his son to drink from his own: to find delight in his wife. The water images reverse in 9:17, where Folly says 'Water you steal tastes sweet.' Rabbinic and Christian readers sometimes took the cistern as one's own Torah study or one's own teacher, but the plain sense is marriage.

a: Should your springs spill out into the street
p: The Hebrew has no question marker. Most read a question; the Greek makes it a prohibition.
b: Read as a statement, 5:16 would tell the son to let his springs flow out into the streets, perhaps meaning many children, which does not fit 5:17. So most translations read a rhetorical question: should your water run in the streets for anyone? The answer is no (5:17). The Greek adds 'not' to the first line: 'Let not water overflow from your spring.' The 'springs' may be the wife's love shared with others, or the man's own strength spent on other women.

a: the woman you married when you were young
p: The phrase 'wife of your youth' returns in Malachi's warning against divorce.
b: Eshet ne'urekha, literally 'the wife of your youth', is the wife a man married young and grew old with. Malachi 2:14–15 uses it of a covenant that the LORD witnessed: do not be faithless to the wife of your youth. Proverbs 2:17 describes the strange woman as having left 'the close friend she had when she was young'. Here the father blesses married love openly: 'let your spring be blessed', and take joy in her.

a: A doe to love, an ibex full of charm
p: Graceful wild animals were terms of endearment, as in the Song of Songs.
b: The doe (ayyalah) and the mountain goat or ibex (ya'alah) are animals of the hills, admired for grace and swiftness; the Song of Songs compares the lover to a gazelle or young stag (Song of Songs 2:9, 17). Love poetry in Egypt and the Near East used the same kind of images. The verse is unembarrassed about physical love: her breasts should give him his fill at all times, using the verb for drinking deeply (yeravvukha), the water image of 5:15–18. The name Jael (Ya'el, 'ibex') shows the word was also a woman's name.
orig: אילת אהבים ויעלת חן (ayyelet ahavim veya'alat chen)
r: Song of Songs 2:9; Song of Songs 2:17; Song of Songs 4:5; Judges 4:17

a: be lost in love for her always
p: The verb shagah, 'stray, reel, be lost', ties 5:19, 5:20 and 5:23 together.
b: Shagah means to stagger or wander, as a drunk man does (20:1; Isaiah 28:7), and so 'be intoxicated' or 'be lost' in something. The father uses it three times: be lost in your wife's love (5:19); why be lost in a strange woman (5:20)? The man without discipline 'is lost' in the greatness of his folly (5:23). The same rapture can be a blessing or a ruin, depending on whom it is for. The Plain keeps 'lost' in all three verses so the wordplay can be followed.

a: he weighs every track he takes
p: The only mention of the LORD in chapter 5: sin in secret is not secret from him.
b: The verb palles, 'level, weigh', is the one used of the woman who does not 'take the level road' (5:6) and of the son who must 'level' his track (4:26). Here the LORD is the surveyor of every road. Job asks, "Is he not watching my ways" (Job 31:4)? The verse turns the warning from prudence to faith: the affair is not only foolish but done in God's sight (compare Joseph's words, Genesis 39:9).

a: the ropes of his sin will hold him tight
p: Sin is its own punishment: the wicked man is snared by what he did.
b: Proverbs often says that evil comes back on the one who does it: the gang sets a trap for its own blood (1:18), and whoever digs a pit falls into it (26:27). Here sin is pictured as ropes or cords (chavlei) that bind the sinner. Psalm 7:15–16 and Psalm 9:15–16 say the same. Many scholars call this the 'deed-consequence' view of Proverbs: actions carry their results within them, and the LORD sees that they do.

a: if you have stood good for your neighbor
p: To 'stand good' for someone was to promise to pay his debt if he did not. Proverbs warns against it again and again.
b: The verb 'arav means to stand as pledge for someone: Judah offers himself as surety for Benjamin (Genesis 43:9; Genesis 44:32). The deal was sealed by 'striking palms' (taqa' kaf), a handshake before witnesses (17:18 'strikes palms'; 22:26 'clap hands'). The Plain says 'stand good for' wherever 'arav has this sense (11:15; 17:18; 20:16; 22:26; 27:13). If the borrower defaulted, the guarantor could lose his property, even his bed (22:27), or be enslaved. Proverbs condemns the practice at least six times (11:15; 17:18; 20:16; 22:26–27; 27:13). The advice is not against generosity but against promising what one cannot control. Hebrews 7:22 later calls Jesus the 'guarantor' of a better covenant, using the Greek word for a surety.
orig: ערבת לרעך (arafta lere'ekha); תקעת לזר כפיך (taqa'ta lazzar kappekha)

a: an outsider
p: The two lines may mean the same person, or two cases: a friend and a stranger.
b: Zar is the masculine of the word used for the 'strange woman' (2:16): someone outside one's own household. If the lines are parallel, the 'neighbor' and the 'outsider' are the same man; or the second line may mean striking hands with a stranger, a creditor, on the neighbor's behalf. Either way the son has put his household at the mercy of people outside it, which links this warning to the warnings about the strange woman.

a: go, throw yourself down, and badger your neighbor
p: The father's advice is to humble yourself and pester the man until he lets you off.
b: Hitrappes is a rare verb, perhaps 'trample yourself' or 'humble yourself'; rehav means 'press hard, storm at'. The son has 'landed in his neighbor's palm', that is, in his power. He must not sleep until he is free (6:4–5), even at the cost of his dignity. The advice is practical: a guarantee may be undone by pleading before the debt falls due.

a: Go to the ant, you lazy one
p: The ant was the model of foresight across the ancient world.
b: The harvester ants of the Middle East gather seeds in summer and store them underground. 30:25 praises them again among 'four things small on the earth'. Greek and Latin writers used the ant the same way, as in Aesop's fable of the ant and the grasshopper. The 'atsel, 'lazy one', is a stock character of Proverbs (10:26; 19:24; 22:13; 26:13–16), more comic than wicked. The Greek adds a second example, the bee (see the variant at 6:8).
orig: לך אל נמלה עצל (lekh el nemalah 'atsel)

a: no official, no ruler
p: The ant works without anyone giving orders: a lesson for the person who waits to be told.
b: Qatsin is a commander or chief (Joshua 10:24), shoter an officer who kept records and drove workers (Exodus 5:6), and moshel a ruler. The point is self-discipline. Ancient writers did not know that ant colonies have a queen, but the observation is true as far as it goes: no ant commands another. Rashi reads the lesson as how much more a human, who has teachers, should work.

a: A little sleep, a little drowsing
p: 6:10–11 appear again, nearly word for word, in 24:33–34, after the story of the lazy one's field.
b: In chapter 24 the teacher passes a field overgrown with thorns and draws the lesson in these same words (24:30–34). The repetition shows that sayings circulated on their own and were set into different collections. The lazy one's words are a mock-quotation: just a little more sleep, the excuse of every late riser.

a: your lack like a man with a shield
t: Like a drifter, like an armed man
p: Poverty arrives like a vagabond and takes what it wants like an armed robber.
b: Mehallekh is 'one who walks about', a vagrant or highwayman; ish magen is 'a man of the shield', an armed man. Poverty comes suddenly and cannot be resisted. The Greek renders 'like a bad traveler' and 'like a good runner', and adds a verse of promise to the diligent (see the variant).

a: A worthless man
p: Adam beliyya'al, 'worthless man', is the phrase that later became the name 'Belial'.
b: Beliyya'al probably means 'without worth' or 'good-for-nothing', and is used for troublemakers and rebels (Deuteronomy 13:13; 1 Samuel 2:12, of Eli's sons; 1 Samuel 25:17, of Nabal). In the Dead Sea Scrolls and in 2 Corinthians 6:15 Belial is a name for the prince of evil. Here he is a smooth troublemaker whose body language (6:13) does what his words do not say.

a: He winks with his eyes
p: Winking, shuffling and pointing are signs given in secret to accomplices.
b: The troublemaker signals with eye, foot and finger, so that what he means differs from what he says (10:10; 16:30; Psalm 35:19). Some think the gestures are those of a sorcerer casting a spell; most take them as secret signals of deceit. Isaiah 58:9 likewise condemns 'pointing the finger'. The written and spoken Hebrew text differ slightly in spelling here, without change of sense.

a: The LORD hates six things
p: A numerical saying: 'six, and seven' means a list that is complete and climaxes in the last item.
b: The pattern 'three, and four' or 'six, and seven' appears in 30:15–31, Job 5:19 and Amos 1–2, and in the Ugaritic poems. The seven items move through the body: eyes, tongue, hands, heart, feet, and then two kinds of people, the lying witness and the one who sows quarrels. The last is the climax: what the LORD hates most here is the destruction of community. The list is not the same as the later Christian list of seven deadly sins. 'Abhorrent to his very self' renders to'avat nafsho, 'an abomination of his soul'.
orig: שש הנה שנא יהוה ושבע תועבת נפשו (shesh hennah sane YHWH vesheva' to'avat nafsho)

a: a lying witness who breathes out lies
p: The ninth commandment in the language of the law court.
b: Yafiach kezavim, 'he breathes out lies', is a phrase found almost only in Proverbs (14:5, 25; 19:5, 9). In a world without forensic evidence, a court depended on witnesses, and the law forbids false testimony (Exodus 20:16; Deuteronomy 19:16–21). The Hebrew piles up two words for lies in one line, and the two phrases name one person, as the Plain's order shows. This is the sixth of the seven; the seventh, the one who sets brothers quarreling, is the 'troublemaker' of 6:14.
orig: יפיח כזבים עד שקר (yafiach kezavim 'ed shaqer)

a: As you walk about, it will guide you
p: The father's teaching walks, sleeps and wakes with the son, in the words of Deuteronomy 6.
b: Deuteronomy 6:6–8 tells Israel to speak of the LORD's words "when you are out on the road, when you go to bed and when you get up" (Deuteronomy 6:7), and to tie them on the hand and between the eyes. Proverbs 6:21–22 uses the same verbs: tie them, walk, lie down, wake. The Mishnah reads the three phrases as three stages: in this world it guides you, in the grave it watches over you, and in the world to come it speaks with you (Mishnah Avot 6:9). Note that 6:22 says 'it', singular, perhaps meaning the teaching as a whole.

a: A command is a lamp, teaching is light
p: The Talmud compares a commandment to a lamp, which lights a moment, and the Torah to daylight, which lasts.
b: Psalm 119:105 says, "A lamp for my foot is your word." Here 'command' (mitsvah) and 'teaching' (torah) are the father's, but the words are the words of the covenant. The Talmud draws a distinction: a good deed protects for a while, like a lamp, but Torah protects always, like the light of the sun (Bavli Sotah 21a). The Greek reads 'the command of the law is a lamp'.
orig: נר מצוה ותורה אור (ner mitsvah vetorah or)

a: A prostitute may cost a round of bread
t: A prostitute and a married woman
p: The Hebrew is hard. Most read a contrast of costs: a prostitute takes your bread, a wife takes your life.
b: The first line is literally 'for on account of a prostitute, up to a loaf of bread'. Readers take it in three main ways: (1) a prostitute costs only a loaf, but another man's wife costs your life (most moderns; the Greek agrees: 'the price of a prostitute is as much as one loaf'); (2) because of a prostitute a man is reduced to a loaf of bread, that is, to poverty (older Jewish and Christian readers, and the King James Version); (3) a textual change. The verse does not approve of prostitution (see 23:27; 29:3); it argues that adultery is far worse because a husband will take revenge (6:34). The 'precious life' that she hunts is the young man himself.
orig: בעד אשה זונה עד ככר לחם (be'ad ishah zonah ad kikkar lachem)

a: Can a man rake fire up against his chest
p: Hebrew ish 'man' and esh 'fire' sound alike, so the question is a pun.
b: Hayachteh ish esh becheqo: 'Can a man take fire into his lap?' The cheq is the fold of the robe at the chest, where things were carried. The pun on ish and esh makes the point: put a man and fire together and he burns. The second question (6:28) pictures walking on coals. Both are about consequences that cannot be avoided once one has acted.
orig: היחתה איש אש בחיקו (hayachteh ish esh becheqo)

a: he must repay seven times over
p: The law of Moses requires a thief to repay double, or four or five times for animals. Why 'seven' here?
b: Exodus 22 sets the penalties: "five cattle in place of the ox and four sheep in place of the sheep" (Exodus 22:1), and "two for one" if the stolen animal is found alive (Exodus 22:4). Proverbs' 'seven times' is probably a figure for full repayment, as seven often means completeness, and 'every last thing his household owns' (6:31) shows that the thief may be ruined. The point is the contrast: a thief can repay, even if it costs him everything; an adulterer has no payment the husband will accept (6:35). Some think the saying comes from a time or place with harsher laws than those in Exodus.

a: A man who commits adultery with a woman is senseless
p: Chasar lev, 'lacking heart', is Proverbs' word for a man without sense; the adulterer is the clearest case.
b: Chasar lev is literally 'lacking heart', that is, lacking judgment (7:7; 9:4, 16; 10:13). Apart from 30:20, this is the only place in Proverbs where the root na'af, 'commit adultery', the verb of the seventh commandment (Exodus 20:14), describes the young man's act. The father's argument is not only 'it is forbidden' but 'it is stupid': the adulterer destroys himself (mashchit nafsho).
orig: נאף אשה חסר לב (no'ef ishah chasar lev)

a: Jealousy is the fury of a man
p: The husband has the right to demand punishment, and he will not accept money instead.
b: Qin'ah is the burning jealousy of a husband (Numbers 5:14), the same word used of God's jealousy for his people (Exodus 20:5). 'The day of revenge' may be the day the case comes to court. 6:35 says he will not accept any kofer, 'ransom' or compensation; the law forbids ransom for a murderer (Numbers 35:31), and the husband treats adultery the same way. The world pictured is one where the wronged husband's choice decides the outcome, as in some ancient Near Eastern laws, such as the Laws of Hammurabi 129, which let the husband spare his wife and so her lover.
r: 6:35; Numbers 5:14; Numbers 35:31; Exodus 21:30; Song of Songs 8:6

a: as you guard the pupil of your eye
t: The little man of the eye
p: The Hebrew word for the pupil means 'little man', from the tiny reflection one sees in another's eye.
b: Ishon 'ayin is literally 'the little man of the eye'. The same phrase describes how the LORD guarded Israel in the wilderness: "he guarded him like the pupil of his eye" (Deuteronomy 32:10; compare Psalm 17:8). English 'pupil' comes from Latin pupilla, 'little doll', for the same reason. The son is to guard the teaching as instinctively as one shields the eye. The first line, 'Keep my commands and live', repeats 4:4 word for word.

a: Tie them on your fingers
p: Perhaps rings, or a reminder tied to the hand, as Deuteronomy commands for the LORD's words.
b: Deuteronomy 6:8 says to tie the commandments 'as a sign on your hand', which Jewish practice fulfills with tefillin, the small leather boxes bound on the arm and head. Proverbs speaks of the fingers, perhaps a ring with an inscription, or straps wound around the fingers, as is done with tefillin today. The second line, 'write them on your heart's tablet', repeats 3:3 and recalls Jeremiah's new covenant, written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33).

a: Tell wisdom, "You are my sister,"
p: In ancient love poetry 'sister' meant 'beloved, bride'. The son is to court Wisdom instead of the stranger.
b: The Song of Songs calls the bride 'my sister, my bride' (Song of Songs 4:9–10, 12), and Egyptian love songs use 'sister' and 'brother' for lovers. The son is told to make Wisdom his beloved, so that she will guard him from the strange woman (7:5). 'Kinswoman' (moda') is a close relative or intimate friend, the word used for Boaz as Naomi's relative (Ruth 2:1). Wisdom is to be family, not a visitor.
r: Song of Songs 4:9–10; Song of Songs 5:1; Ruth 2:1; 4:6–9; Wisdom of Solomon 8:2

a: Once, from my house window
p: The father looks out through a lattice. In the Greek it is the woman herself who leans out of her window.
b: Challon is a window and eshnav a lattice, a wooden grille that let a person see out without being seen; Sisera's mother looks through one (Judges 5:28), and Jezebel looks out of a window (2 Kings 9:30). Ivory carvings from Phoenicia and Samaria show a 'woman at the window', a motif some connect with a goddess or with prostitution. In the Hebrew the father is the watcher. The Greek reads 'from a window of her house she peeks out into the streets', making the woman the one at the window (see the variant). The whole scene, 7:6–23, is told as something the father saw.
orig: בחלון ביתי בעד אשנבי (bechallon beti be'ad eshnabbi)
r: Judges 5:28; 2 Kings 9:30; 2 Samuel 6:16; Song of Songs 2:9

a: at dusk, in the evening of the day
p: Four time words move from twilight to deepest night as the young man walks toward her house.
b: Neshef (twilight), 'erev yom (evening of the day), ishon laylah (the 'pupil' of the night, its blackest point, the same word as in 7:2) and afelah (gloom). The poet slows the scene so that the reader sees him go deeper into darkness. The darkness is literal (adultery seeks the night, Job 24:15) and moral, the dark road of 4:19.
orig: בנשף בערב יום באישון לילה ואפלה (beneshef be'erev yom be'ishon laylah va'afelah)

a: in a prostitute's clothes, her heart kept hidden
p: She is a married woman (7:19) dressed like a prostitute; her heart is 'guarded', that is, she hides her intentions.
b: Shit zonah, 'the dress of a prostitute', may have been a recognizable style; Tamar dressed to be taken for one (Genesis 38:14–15). Netsurat lev, 'guarded of heart', means crafty, keeping her real purpose hidden. The phrase is ironic, because the son was told to 'guard' his own heart (4:23). The woman is the opposite of the woman of 31:10–31, whose household is clothed in scarlet and who is clothed with strength.
orig: שית זונה ונצרת לב (shit zonah unetsurat lev)

a: her feet will not settle in her house
p: The woman is loud, restless and always out in public. Modern readers ask what this teaches about women.
b: The poet describes her by the opposite of what his society praised in a wife: she is 'noisy' (homiyyah, the word used of Folly in 9:13), 'headstrong' or 'unruly' (sorarat), and wandering the streets instead of staying at home. Feminist scholars point out that the poem is written by men for young men and turns a woman's freedom of movement into a sign of danger (Newsom; Yee). Others answer that the poem judges her for deceit and adultery, not for being a woman, and that Proverbs also praises a wife who goes out to buy a field and trade (31:16–24) and condemns male seducers and violent men as strongly (1:10–19). Both points can be held together: the warnings are real, and they are drawn from a man's point of view.

a: Sacrifices of peace offerings were due from me
p: Peace-offering meat had to be eaten within a day or two. She has meat at home and invites him to share it.
b: The shelamim or peace offering was a sacrifice shared between God, the priests and the worshiper, who ate most of the meat with family and friends. A vow offering could be eaten on the day of the sacrifice and the next day (Leviticus 7:15–16). So her words mean: I have fulfilled my vows, there is a feast waiting, come and eat. Some scholars once thought she was a devotee of a foreign love goddess paying a vow by sleeping with a stranger (Boström), but most now see an Israelite wife using religious language to dress up an affair. Her piety makes the deception worse.

a: with myrrh, aloes and cinnamon
p: Expensive imported perfumes: the same spices appear in the Song of Songs and in Psalm 45.
b: Myrrh came from Arabia and East Africa, aloes (perhaps eaglewood) from India, and cinnamon from South Asia, through long trade routes. Psalm 45:8 mentions the king's robes fragrant with myrrh and aloes, and the Song of Songs lists myrrh, aloes and cinnamon in the bride's garden (Song of Songs 4:14). The bedspreads of 'Egyptian linen' (7:16) were luxury cloth too. The scene is designed to impress a young man from an ordinary home.
r: 7:16; Psalm 45:8; Song of Songs 4:14; Song of Songs 3:6; Exodus 30:23; John 19:39

a: let's soak ourselves in love until morning
p: Her invitation uses the words of the Song of Songs: dodim 'lovemaking', ahavim 'love'.
b: Nirveh dodim, 'let us drink our fill of love', uses the plural dodim, the word for physical love in Song of Songs 1:2 and 4:10 ('your love is better than wine'). The father has already used the same verb for married love: 'let her breasts give you your fill' (yeravvukha, 5:19). She offers what the father commanded the son to find at home.
r: 5:19; Song of Songs 1:2; Song of Songs 4:10; Song of Songs 5:1

a: The man of the house is away
p: She calls her husband 'the man', not 'my husband': a small word that shows her distance from him.
b: The Hebrew says ha'ish, 'the man', with the article, where one would expect ishi, 'my husband'. The Greek restores 'my husband'. He has taken 'the money pouch' (7:20), so he is away on a long business trip and will return only at the full moon (keseh, Psalm 81:3), perhaps two weeks. She is a married woman of means, not a poor prostitute; this is why the father calls the danger adultery.

a: like a stubborn fool in shackles going off to be punished
p: The Hebrew of this line is hard; many scholars correct it to 'like a stag bounding into a noose'.
b: The Hebrew reads ukhe'ekhes el musar 'evil, literally 'and like an anklet to the discipline of a fool'. 'Ekhes is an anklet (Isaiah 3:18), and the line seems to mean a stubborn fool ('evil, as in 1:7) led in fetters to punishment. Musar, elsewhere 'discipline', here means correction by punishment, so the Plain says 'to be punished'. But the next verse speaks of an arrow and a bird, so many scholars read ke'ayyal, 'like a stag', for 'evil, 'fool', and 'akhas, 'leaping', giving 'like a stag bounding into a noose' to match the ox (7:22b) and the bird (7:23b). The Greek has 'like a dog to bonds' and then 'or like a deer struck in the liver by an arrow'. The Plain follows the Hebrew; see the variant.
orig: וכעכס אל מוסר אויל (ukhe'ekhes el musar 'evil)

a: until an arrow slices through his liver
p: In Hebrew thought the liver, like the heart, was a seat of life; an arrow there is fatal.
b: Kaved, the liver, is named as the inner organ that pours out in grief (Lamentations 2:11); in Mesopotamia diviners read the livers of sacrificed sheep to learn the future. The young man is like an ox, a hunted animal and a bird in a trap: three pictures of a creature that walks into death without knowing. 'His life is at stake' renders benafsho hu, 'it is for his life'.
orig: עד יפלח חץ כבדו (ad yefallach chets kevedo)

a: Roads to Sheol, that is her house
t: A house that is a road to death
p: Her house is not a home but a crossroads leading down to the underworld.
b: The chapter ends as 2:18–19 and 5:5 do: the strange woman's house leads to Sheol and the 'bedrooms of death' (chadrei mavet), a grim echo of her perfumed bed (7:16–17). The contrast is set up for chapters 8–9: Wisdom's house has seven pillars and a feast (9:1–6), while Folly's guests are 'down in Sheol's depths' (9:18). The Qumran poem known as 'The Wiles of the Wicked Woman' (4Q184) develops this picture at length, making her a figure of evil itself.
orig: דרכי שאול ביתה (darkhei she'ol betah); חדרי מות (chadrei mavet)

a: Is that not Wisdom calling
p: Unlike the strange woman, who whispers at dusk, Wisdom calls aloud at the busiest places in town.
b: Chapter 8 answers chapter 7. The strange woman lurks at corners in the dark (7:8–12); Wisdom stands on the heights, at the crossroads and at the city gates (8:2–3), the places of trade and law, in daylight. Her message is for everyone (8:4). She speaks as a prophet does (compare 1:20–33), but she does not say 'Thus says the LORD': she speaks in her own name, as no other figure in the Bible does except God.

a: fools, understand with your heart
p: Literally 'understand heart': gain a mind, get sense.
b: Havinu lev, 'understand heart', means to acquire the sense one lacks; the senseless one in Proverbs 'lacks heart' (7:7; 9:4). The Greek reads 'you who are undisciplined, put in a heart'. 'Naive' (peta'im) and 'fools' (kesilim) are the two groups Wisdom addressed in 1:22. She does not start with the wise but with those who most need her.

a: princely things
p: Negidim may mean 'princely, noble things' or 'straightforward things'.
b: Negidim usually means 'leaders, princes' (as in 28:16), so 'noble things'. But it may come from neged, 'in front, opposite', and mean 'plain, straightforward things', which fits 8:8–9: her words are 'plain' and 'level'. The Greek has 'solemn things' (semna). Either way Wisdom contrasts her speech with the 'smooth' words of the strange woman (7:21).

a: For wisdom is better than red coral
p: 8:11 repeats 3:15 almost exactly, but speaks of Wisdom in the third person in the middle of her own speech.
b: Compare 3:15: 'She is worth more than red coral; of all the things you want, none is her equal.' Because 8:11 says 'wisdom' and 'her' while Wisdom is speaking in the first person, many scholars think it was added by an editor, borrowed from 3:15. Others accept the shift as normal in Hebrew poetry. The Plain matches the wording of 3:15 where the Hebrew is the same.

a: The fear of the LORD means hating evil.
p: The first line sounds like a teacher's comment set into Wisdom's speech.
b: This line names 'the fear of the LORD' in the third person and then Wisdom resumes: 'I hate them.' Some think it is an editor's gloss explaining what Wisdom's hatred of pride means. Others take it as Wisdom quoting the book's motto (1:7). Either way it defines the fear of the LORD morally: not terror but the hatred of evil, as in Job 28:28, "to keep away from evil, that is understanding."
orig: יראת יהוה שנאת רע (yir'at YHWH sene'at ra')

a: It is through me that kings are kings
p: Kings rule well by wisdom. Ancient kings claimed wisdom from the gods; here Wisdom herself gives it.
b: In Egypt and Mesopotamia, kings presented themselves as wise judges gifted by the gods, as Hammurabi does in the prologue to his laws. Israel's model is Solomon, who asked for "a heart that listens" (1 Kings 3:9) so that he could judge and whose wisdom made him great (1 Kings 3:28). Isaiah 11:2 promises a king on whom will rest 'the spirit of wisdom and understanding'. 8:15–16 means not that every king is wise, but that every good law depends on Wisdom. The Greek and later readers applied the verse to God's choice of rulers (compare Daniel 2:21; Romans 13:1).

a: Those who love me, I love
p: Wisdom answers love with love, and the seeker who 'looks for her early' finds her.
b: The verb shichar, 'hunt hard for', is related to shachar, 'dawn', and older translations rendered 'those who seek me early'. It means to look for something eagerly. The promise reverses 1:28, where those who refused Wisdom 'will hunt hard for me and never find me' (the same verb). Jesus' 'Seek and you will find' (Matthew 7:7) and Wisdom of Solomon 6:12, where Wisdom is easily seen by those who love her, carry the thought on. In the written Hebrew the first line reads 'those who love her'; see the variant.
orig: אני אהבי אהב ומשחרי ימצאנני (ani ohavai ehav umeshacharai yimtsa'uneni)

a: inherit real wealth
p: Yesh means 'what exists, substance': the wealth Wisdom gives is lasting, not imaginary.
b: Yesh, 'there is', is used here as a noun: 'substance, property', the opposite of something that vanishes (23:5). Wisdom's wealth includes material riches (8:18), but the emphasis is on what truly lasts. The Greek adds a line after 8:21: 'If I tell you the things that happen daily, I will remember to recount the things from of old', a bridge to the account of creation that follows. The last teaching of the Mishnah reads yesh by the numerical value of its letters, 310, and says that God will give each righteous person 310 worlds (Mishnah Uktsin 3:12).

a: The LORD acquired me
