p: Qanah can mean 'acquire', 'create' or 'father'. Which is meant here has been argued for two thousand years.
b: Qanah usually means 'acquire, get, buy', as in 4:5 and 4:7 ('Acquire wisdom'). In a few places it seems to mean 'create' or 'make': God Most High is qoneh of heaven and earth, 'maker of heaven and earth' (Genesis 14:19, 22), and the LORD is Israel's father 'who brought you into being' (Deuteronomy 32:6). In Genesis 4:1 Eve names Cain because 'I have gained a man', and the verb there is close to 'bear, produce'. In 8:24–25 Wisdom says she was 'born', so many read 'fathered' or 'brought forth' here. The Greek, the Syriac and the Targum have 'created'; Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion have 'acquired'; Jerome's Latin has 'possessed' (possedit), as reported by Toy. The Plain uses 'acquired', the verb's usual sense and the one used in chapter 4 (see Claude's note on the book page); 'created' and 'fathered' remain possible.

a: the first of his way
p: Reshit darko: Wisdom is the first thing God made or acquired, or the beginning of his activity.
b: Reshit, 'beginning, first', is the word of Genesis 1:1, bereshit, 'in the beginning'. 'His way' may be his acting in the world. The phrase can be read as a title, 'the first of his way', or as a time, 'at the beginning of his way'. Job 40:19 calls Behemoth 'the first of God's ways' with the same words. The Greek has 'a beginning of his ways for his works', and Revelation 3:14 calls Christ 'the beginning (archē) of God's creation', using the Greek word of this verse; the site's Plain there reads "the ruler of God's creation."

a: The LORD acquired me, the first of his way
t: Wisdom and the Son: the Arian controversy
p: Early Christians read Wisdom as Christ. In the 300s Arius argued from 'created me' that the Son was a creature.
b: Paul calls Christ 'the wisdom of God' (1 Corinthians 1:24), and Colossians 1:15–17 calls him 'the firstborn of all creation'. Justin (Dialogue with Trypho 61) and Tertullian (Against Praxeas 6–7) quoted Proverbs 8 to show that the Son was begotten before creation. But the Greek said 'The Lord created me'. About 318, Arius of Alexandria taught that before the Son 'was begotten or created or determined or founded, he was not', echoing the verbs of 8:22–25 in Greek. The Council of Nicaea (325) answered that the Son is 'begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father', and condemned those who say 'there was when he was not'. Athanasius replied that 'created' refers to the human nature the Son took on 'for his works' of salvation, while 'he begets me' (8:25) speaks of his eternal birth (Orations against the Arians 2.44–82). See the chapter page.
r: 8:25; 1 Corinthians 1:24; 1 Corinthians 1:30; Colossians 1:15–17; John 1:1–3; Hebrews 1:2–3; Revelation 3:14

a: before his works of long ago
p: The rabbis heard Wisdom as the Torah, which God 'acquired' first and used as the plan for creating the world.
b: Sirach 24 has Wisdom tell how she came from the mouth of the Most High and settled in Israel, and then says, 'All this is the book of the covenant of the Most High God, the law that Moses commanded us' (Sirach 24:23). Baruch 4:1 says the same. The rabbis took this further. The Mishnah lists five things God 'acquired' in his world and names the Torah first, proving it from 8:22 (Mishnah Avot 6:10). Genesis Rabbah 1:1 reads 'the first' (reshit) of 8:22 together with Genesis 1:1: 'with reshit God created', that is, with the Torah. Rabbi Akiva called the Torah 'the precious instrument by which the world was created' (Mishnah Avot 3:14). See the note on 8:30.

a: I was installed
p: Nissakhti may mean 'I was set up', as a king is, or 'I was woven', as a child is in the womb.
b: One root, nasakh, gives 'I have installed my king' in Psalm 2:6 ("I myself have put my king in place"), so Wisdom would be enthroned from of old. Another root, sakhakh, gives 'you wove me together in my mother's womb' (Psalm 139:13), which fits the birth language of 8:24–25. Many modern scholars prefer 'woven' or 'formed'. The Greek has 'he founded me' (ethemeliōsen), a word Arius later used. Jerome's Latin, in the critical Stuttgart text, has ordita sum, from ordior, 'begin a web, lay the warp', which supports 'woven'; the Clementine text has ordinata sum, 'I was set up', as Toy reports.

a: Before there were any deeps, I was born
p: Cholalti means 'I was brought forth', a word for birth labor. Wisdom was born before the world.
b: Cholalti, from chil, 'writhe in labor', is used of giving birth (Job 15:7, "Were you birthed before the hills?"; Psalm 90:2, of the mountains being born). It returns in 8:25. The language is metaphor: no mother is named, and the poem does not say how Wisdom was born of God. But together with 'acquired' (8:22) and 'woven' (8:23), it presents Wisdom as God's child, older than the deep, the springs, the mountains and the earth itself. Compare the creation of Genesis 1:2, where 'darkness lay on the face of the deep'.

a: I was there when he fixed the heavens in place
p: Wisdom watched the making of the world. John 1, Colossians 1 and Hebrews 1 say the same of the Son.
b: Job 38:4 asks Job where he was when God laid the earth's foundation; Wisdom can answer, 'I was there.' 8:27–29 follows the order of creation: the heavens, the circle of the horizon, the clouds, the springs, the limit of the sea and the foundations of the earth. John 1:1–3 says that the Word was with God in the beginning and that all things came into being through him; Hebrews 1:2–3 calls the Son the one through whom God made the worlds, the radiance of his glory; Wisdom of Solomon 7:25–26 calls Wisdom 'a reflection of eternal light'. Most scholars agree that these New Testament passages draw on the language of Wisdom.
r: Job 38:4–11; John 1:1–3; Colossians 1:15–17; Hebrews 1:2–3; Wisdom of Solomon 7:22–26; Wisdom of Solomon 9:9; Psalm 104:24

a: when he carved a circle on the surface of the deep
p: The horizon, pictured as a circle drawn on the ocean, marking where sky meets sea.
b: Chug is a circle or vault. Job 26:10 says God "has traced a ring across the surface of the waters, where light and darkness reach their end", and Isaiah 40:22 speaks of God enthroned 'above the circle of the earth'. Ancient Israelites, like their neighbors, pictured the earth as land set within a great ocean, with the sky as a dome whose edge rested on the horizon. The verb 'carved' (chuq) is the root of 'decree': God draws the line and orders the waters to keep to it (8:29).
orig: בחוקו חוג על פני תהום (bechuqo chug 'al penei tehom)

a: when he laid down for the sea its fixed line
p: God sets a limit the sea may not cross, a theme of Job, Psalms and Jeremiah.
b: The LORD in Job says, "when I carved out my boundary for it and put up a bolt and doors" (Job 38:10). Psalm 104:9 and Jeremiah 5:22 also speak of the boundary of the sand. Behind these lines lies the older picture of creation as God's mastery of the unruly sea (Psalm 74:13–14; Job 26:12). In Proverbs there is no battle: the sea simply obeys 'what his mouth ordered'. Two of the three lines of this verse are missing from Codex Vaticanus (see the variant).
r: Job 38:8–11; Job 26:12; Psalm 104:9; Jeremiah 5:22; Psalm 74:13–14; Genesis 1:9–10

a: a craftsman
p: A hard word: Wisdom was beside God as a master builder, a nursing child, or a constant companion.
b: The Hebrew 'amon has been read in three main ways. (1) Craftsman, master builder: compare 'omman, 'artisan' (Song of Songs 7:1), and Akkadian ummānu, 'expert, sage'. Wisdom of Solomon 7:22 calls Wisdom 'the fashioner of all things', and the Plain follows this sense. (2) Child, 'nursling': reading 'amun, from 'aman, 'nurse, bring up' (Numbers 11:12; Lamentations 4:5). Aquila has 'being nursed', and this fits 'playing' and 'delight' in 8:30–31. (3) Faithfully, constantly: reading 'emun, 'faithfulness', as the Targum does. The Greek has 'joining things together' (harmozousa); Jerome's Latin, 'arranging all things' (cuncta componens); Symmachus and Theodotion, 'established' (versions as reported by Toy).
r: Song of Songs 7:1; Jeremiah 52:15; Numbers 11:12; Lamentations 4:5; Wisdom of Solomon 7:22; Wisdom of Solomon 8:6

a: And I was at his side, a craftsman.
p: Genesis Rabbah 1:1 reads 'amon as 'artisan' and Wisdom as the Torah: God used it as an architect uses a plan.
b: The midrash opens with this verse. Rabbi Hoshaiah gives several meanings of 'amon: 'pedagogue' (a child's guardian), 'covered', 'hidden', 'great', and finally 'artisan' (uman). Then the Torah speaks: 'I was the craftsman's tool of the Holy One.' A human king who builds a palace does not build it from his own head but from a plan; 'so the Holy One looked into the Torah and created the world' (Genesis Rabbah 1:1). Philo of Alexandria, centuries earlier, called Wisdom the mother through whom the universe came into being, and quoted 8:22. The Jewish and Christian readings share the idea of a pre-existent agent of creation, and differ on who that agent is.

a: I was delight, day after day
p: Egyptian texts picture Maat, goddess of order, as the creator's beloved child. Most see real influence on the imagery.
b: Christa Kayatz showed that Egyptian texts describe Maat, the order of the world, as the daughter of the sun god, embraced by him and his delight, present when he made the world, and given to kings so that they rule justly. Proverbs 8 has the same features: beloved child, delight, presence at creation, and the source of good government (8:15–16). Others compare the Isis hymns of the Greek world, in which the goddess praises herself in the first person. The verdict of most scholars: the poet borrowed images from Egypt but made Wisdom the LORD's creature or child, not a goddess. Bernhard Lang argued that a real Hebrew goddess of wisdom lies behind her; few have followed him.
orig: ואהיה שעשעים יום יום (va'ehyeh sha'ashu'im yom yom)

a: playing in front of him all the time
p: The verb means laughing, playing, dancing. Wisdom's place at creation is joy, not labor.
b: Mesacheqet, 'playing', is from sachaq, 'laugh, play', the root of Isaac's name. It is used of children playing in the streets of the restored Jerusalem (Zechariah 8:5), of David dancing before the ark (2 Samuel 6:21), and of Leviathan sporting in the sea (Psalm 104:26: "Leviathan, which you shaped to sport in it"). Whether Wisdom is a craftsman or a child (see the note above), the picture is of delight shared between God and his creation. 'Delight' (sha'ashu'im) is the word for Ephraim as God's 'darling child' (Jeremiah 31:20).

a: my delights were with human beings
p: Wisdom's joy ends with people. Jewish readers saw here the gift of the Torah to Israel; Christians, the incarnation.
b: The poem moves from God's delight in Wisdom to Wisdom's delight in the world and, last, in benei adam, 'the children of Adam'. This turns her speech back to her listeners (8:32): the Wisdom who was with God before creation wants to live among people. Rabbinic readers connected the line with the Torah's descent to Israel at Sinai. Christian readers took it of the Word who 'became flesh and lived among us' (John 1:14). Sirach 24:8 has Wisdom told, 'Make your dwelling in Jacob.'
orig: ושעשעי את בני אדם (vesha'ashu'ai et benei adam)

a: keeping watch by the posts of my doorways
p: Mezuzot, 'doorposts', is the word for the posts on which Israel wrote the Shema.
b: Deuteronomy 6:9 tells Israel to write God's words 'on the doorposts (mezuzot) of your house', and the small case on Jewish doorposts is still called a mezuzah. Here the disciple stands outside Wisdom's door day after day, like a pupil waiting for a teacher or a lover waiting for his beloved (compare Song of Songs 5:2–4). The picture prepares for chapter 9, where Wisdom's house stands open.

a: The one who finds me has found life
p: The second line has the same Hebrew as 18:22b, said of the man who finds a wife.
b: Vayafeq ratson meYHWH, 'and he obtains favor from the LORD', appears only here and in 18:22, of finding a wife; the Plain's wording here is the model for both. The parallel makes Wisdom the bride a young man should seek (compare 4:6–9; 7:4). Christian readers heard in 'whoever finds me finds life' the words of John's Gospel and letters: the one who has the Son has life (1 John 5:12; John 17:3). In the first line, the written Hebrew reads 'those who find me are finders of life'; the text read aloud has 'whoever finds me has found life' (see the variant).

a: The one who misses me
p: Chata', the common word for 'sin', means first 'to miss': to miss Wisdom is to harm oneself.
b: Chote'i, 'the one who misses me', uses the root of 'sin', whose basic sense is to miss a target, as of the left-handed slingers who "could hit a single hair with a slingstone, never missing" (Judges 20:16). Here the opposite of 'finding' her (8:35) is 'missing' her. The result is not God's anger but self-harm: he 'does violence to his own soul'. The speech ends with a stark choice: Wisdom is life, and hating her is to love death (compare Deuteronomy 30:19).

a: Wisdom has built her house
p: Why seven pillars? The days of creation, the seven parts of Proverbs 1–9, a palace or temple, or the Church.
b: Proposals include: (1) a grand house or palace, since ordinary houses did not need seven pillars; some compare temples with columns and see Wisdom's house as a shrine; (2) the seven days of creation, as the Talmud reads it: 'Wisdom has built her house' is the attribute by which God made the world, and the seven pillars are the seven days (Bavli Sanhedrin 38a); (3) the structure of chapters 1–9 themselves, which Patrick Skehan argued were composed as seven 'columns' of poetry; (4) the seven planets or the cosmos; (5) in Christian reading, Christ's flesh as the house Wisdom built for herself, with the Church joined to it (Augustine, City of God 17.20); later medieval readers added the seven gifts of the Spirit (Isaiah 11:2) or the seven sacraments. The plain sense is a house large enough to hold a feast for everyone she invites.

a: mixed her wine
p: Wine was mixed with water, or with spices, before serving at a feast.
b: Masekhah yeinah: wine in the ancient world was strong and was usually mixed with water in a large bowl before it was served, as the Greek 'mixed in a bowl' shows; it could also be spiced (Song of Songs 8:2). Butchering an animal meant meat, a rare luxury, so Wisdom is giving a banquet, not a snack. The same verbs describe a royal or sacred feast (Isaiah 25:6). Compare 23:30, where 'mixed wine' belongs to the drunkard.

a: She has sent her serving girls out
p: Wisdom sends out her servants to call guests, like the king in Jesus' parable of the wedding feast.
b: Wisdom's young women go out to the 'tops of the town's high places', where she herself called in 8:2. Jesus tells of a king who sends his servants to call people to his son's wedding banquet (Matthew 22:1–10; compare Luke 14:16–24), and of Wisdom who 'is shown right by her children' (Luke 7:35). Isaiah 55:1–3 invites the thirsty to come and buy wine and milk without money. The fathers read Wisdom's servants as the apostles sent to the nations.

a: Who is naive? Let him come over here!
p: Wisdom and Folly both call 'Who is naive?' (9:4 and 9:16). The invitation is the same; the meal is not.
b: 9:4 and 9:16 are identical in Hebrew, and the Plain matches them. Both women sit or stand on the town's heights (9:3, 14) and call the same people. The reader must tell them apart by what they offer: Wisdom's bread and wine bring life (9:6), Folly's stolen water and secret bread lead to Sheol (9:17–18). This is the last lesson of chapters 1–9: two voices will always call, and they will sound alike.
orig: מי פתי יסר הנה (mi feti yasur hennah)

a: Come, have some of my bread
p: Jews read Wisdom's meal as the study of Torah; Christians, from early times, as the Eucharist.
b: The rabbis applied 'eat my bread' to the Torah, as Sirach 24:19–21 has Wisdom say 'Come to me... those who eat me will hunger for more' and Sirach 15:3 speaks of 'the bread of understanding'. Jesus calls himself the bread of life and says that whoever comes to him will not hunger (John 6:35). Many fathers, from Cyprian and Augustine on, read Wisdom's bread and mixed wine as the Lord's Supper, and Wisdom's house as the Church (Augustine, City of God 17.20). Orthodox churches read 9:1–11 at Vespers on feasts of the Mother of God, taking the 'house' as Mary in whom Wisdom took flesh.
r: Sirach 24:19–21; Sirach 15:3; Isaiah 55:1–3; John 6:35; John 6:51; 1 Corinthians 11:23–26

a: Discipline a mocker, and you pick up disgrace for yourself
p: 9:7–12 breaks into the two portraits of Wisdom and Folly with sayings on teaching mockers.
b: The chapter is built in three parts: Wisdom's feast (9:1–6), a set of sayings (9:7–12) and Folly's feast (9:13–18). Many scholars think 9:7–12 was added, since it changes from narrative to short sayings and speaks of the mocker and the wise. Others see it as the hinge: it tells the reader which guest he will be, the wise who welcomes correction (9:8–9) or the mocker who resents it. 9:10 repeats the motto of 1:7 to close the introduction. Jesus' warning not to throw pearls to pigs (Matthew 7:6) makes a similar point to 9:7–8.

a: rebuke the wise, and he will love you for it
p: The mark of the wise is not that they need no rebuke but that they welcome it.
b: Hokhach, 'rebuke, correct', is the word of 3:12. Proverbs often defines the wise and the fool by how they take criticism (12:1; 15:31–32; 19:25). Psalm 141:5 says, "If a righteous man hits me, it is loyal love". The same verb is used of the duty to correct a neighbor in Leviticus 19:17.

a: The start of wisdom is the fear of the LORD
p: The introduction ends as it began (1:7), with the fear of the LORD as the start of wisdom.
b: 1:7 said that the fear of the LORD is 'where knowledge begins' (reshit da'at); 9:10 says it is 'the start of wisdom' (techillat chokhmah), the wording of Psalm 111:10, "Wisdom starts with the fear of the LORD". The repetition frames chapters 1–9. Techillah means the first step in time, which settles the debate over reshit in 1:7 (see the note there) at least for this verse. Job 28:28 makes the same claim. The Greek adds a third line: 'for to know the law is the mark of a good mind.'
orig: תחלת חכמה יראת יהוה (techillat chokhmah yir'at YHWH)

a: knowing the Holy One is understanding
p: Qedoshim, literally 'holy ones', is a plural used as a title for God, as in 30:3.
b: The plural qedoshim stands in parallel with 'the LORD', so it is a plural of majesty like Elohim, 'God'; compare 30:3 and Hosea 11:12. The Greek read it as real plural, 'the counsel of the holy ones' or 'of saints'. 'Knowing' God, as in 2:5, means a relationship of loyalty, not only facts.

a: It is by me that your days grow many
p: The speaker is Wisdom again, or the father; the verse continues the promise of long life.
b: After 9:10 speaks of Wisdom in the third person, 9:11 says 'by me', so the speaker is probably Wisdom, picking up her speech of 9:4–6, or the teacher who speaks for her. Long life is the reward Proverbs most often promises (3:2, 16; 4:10; 10:27). Proverbs states it as a rule of how life goes; Job and Ecclesiastes ask what to make of the exceptions.

a: if you mock, you will carry it by yourself
t: Wisdom is for your own good
p: Your wisdom or folly affects you above all. The Greek adds that wisdom also helps your neighbors.
b: The verse makes each person responsible for his own character: the wise gain and the mocker bears the cost alone. Job 22:2–3 asks whether a person's righteousness benefits God at all. The Greek adds 'you will be wise for your neighbors as well', and then three more verses about the one who 'shepherds the winds' and 'chases flying birds', wanders from his own vineyard and gathers barrenness with his hands (see the variant).
orig: אם חכמת חכמת לך (im chakhamta chakhamta lakh)

a: Woman Folly is noisy
p: Folly is drawn as a loud woman at her door, a mirror image of Wisdom and a double of the strange woman.
b: Eshet kesilut, 'woman of folly', sits at the door of her house 'on a chair' on the heights (9:14), as Wisdom stands on the heights (9:3). She is 'noisy' like the strange woman (7:11) and calls with Wisdom's own words (9:16). She is 'all naivety' (petayyut, found only here) and 'knows nothing whatever', which may mean she knows no shame, as the Greek has it. Her figure gathers up the strange woman of chapters 2–7 and makes her the symbol of every false path. The Greek says she 'comes to lack a crust of bread', a reversal of Wisdom's feast.

a: Water you steal tastes sweet
p: Folly's slogan: forbidden pleasure is sweeter. In Proverbs' code, water is sex (5:15–18).
b: The father told his son to drink water from his own cistern (5:15); Folly offers stolen water and secret bread. Bread too can be a figure for sex (30:20, where the adulteress 'eats and wipes her mouth'). The saying captures the appeal of the forbidden as old as Genesis 3, where the fruit looked good to eat and desirable. The Greek turns the slogan into a command and adds three verses of warning: 'spring away, do not linger... do not drink from a strange spring' (see the variant at 9:18).

a: He has no idea that the shades are there
p: The last line of chapters 1–9: Folly's guests are already among the dead.
b: The young man thinks he is going to a party; the house is full of 'shades' (refa'im), the dead (2:18; Isaiah 14:9). Wisdom's guests 'live' (9:6); Folly's 'are down in Sheol's depths'. The introduction to Proverbs ends with this choice, and the short sayings that follow in chapter 10 assume the reader has made it. Jesus' picture of the broad road leading to destruction (Matthew 7:13) carries the same warning.
